summary: An April Fools' RFC that takes a humorous look at the tangle of three letter acronyms. It pretends to give IANA considerations so that one acronym does not have several expansions. It is not a real standard and should be read as a joke.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5513 is an April 1st joke about the many meanings of three-letter acronyms. It pretends to create an IANA registry with serious-sounding rules and deliberately silly entries.

subtitle: An April 1st joke about a registry for three-letter acronyms.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke imagines confusion caused when network and protocol acronyms have multiple meanings.
tldr.mechanism: It proposes a pretend Internet TLA Registry with humorous reserved expansions and allocation procedures.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5513 is an Informational joke memo dated April 1, 2009; it does not specify an Internet standard.

today: RFC 5513 is an Informational memo dated April 1, 2009, and does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: The Acronym Problem
sections.content: RFC 5513 is an April 1st joke that uses a real source of confusion as its premise: one three-letter acronym can have multiple expansions. The memo presents a fictional shortage of acronyms and jokes that a document's value can be measured by how many acronyms it contains. It gives TCP and the Internet Stream Protocol as examples.
sections.plainLanguage: This April 1st joke starts from the fact that acronyms can have several meanings. It exaggerates the problem into a fictional shortage.

sections.title: The Pretend TLA Registry
sections.content: The memo proposes an Internet TLA Registry recording each acronym, its unique interpretation, and a defining RFC. It reserves entries with deliberately humorous expansions, including TLA as “Two Letter Acronym” and RFC as “Ready for Compost.” The proposed allocation categories are Experimental Use, First Come First Served, and IETF Review.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed registry has fields for an acronym, its meaning, and its defining RFC. Some reserved meanings and assignment rules are intentionally absurd.

sections.title: Compatibility and Multiple Meanings
sections.content: The RFC jokes that IANA would search existing RFCs for acronym uses and find duplicate meanings. It proposes an intentionally impractical way to resolve collisions by dividing the letters among competing meanings. The memo's examples and mock allocation process maintain its humorous treatment of acronym confusion.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo imagines a search finding many repeated acronyms. Its suggested way to divide them is another part of the joke.
